entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Fan Zhen (c. 450–515 CE) was a pivotal Chinese philosopher, politician, and writer who served under the Southern Qi and Liang dynasties, whose radical materialist and atheist doctrines profoundly challenged the burgeoning influence of Buddhism in 5th and 6th-century China. Born into an intellectual milieu amidst the tumultuous Southern Dynasties period, Fan Zhen held prominent official roles, yet his most enduring contribution was his fervent philosophical opposition to supernaturalism, particularly the Buddhist concept of karma and the immortality of the soul. His work represents a crucial moment in the intellectual history of China, providing a robust, indigenous philosophical counterpoint to the foreign religious ideas that were rapidly gaining imperial patronage and popular adherence.

Fan Zhen's most renowned achievement is his treatise, *Shén Miè Lùn* (神滅論, 'Treatise on the Extinction of the Soul'), written around 490 CE. In this work, he meticulously argued that the "spirit" (shen) is merely a function of the body (xing), just as sharpness is a function of a knife, and therefore perishes with the body's death. This direct refutation of the Buddhist doctrine of transmigration and the immortality of the soul sparked intense controversy, drawing the ire of powerful Buddhist monks and even Emperor Wu of Liang, a devout Buddhist who personally engaged in debates with Fan Zhen, attempting to persuade him to recant his views. Despite immense pressure, including threats and public ostracization, Fan Zhen steadfastly maintained his philosophical position, becoming a symbol of intellectual integrity and resistance against dominant religious dogma.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Fan Zhen's radical materialist philosophy provided a crucial indigenous intellectual challenge to the rapidly spreading Buddhism in 5th-6th century China, influencing later rationalist thought and anti-Buddhist movements. His work forced a significant philosophical debate that shaped the intellectual landscape of medieval China.
